item.title: Choosing a Hardware Wallet for Multisig: What Matters
item.description: The features that matter when a hardware wallet joins a multisig: wallet registration, address and change checks, PSBT, message signing and connections.
item.content:encoded:
Almost every bitcoin hardware wallet can sign for a multisig wallet. Far fewer can protect you inside one. In a 2-of-3 multisig, the hardware wallet is usually the key that stops a compromised phone or computer, so what matters is not the logo but what the device checks and shows on its own screen. This guide lists the features worth looking for, why each one matters, and the questions to ask before you buy. It does not crown a winner: firmware changes often, so check each vendor's current documentation for the features below.

Why multisig asks more of a hardware wallet

With a single-key wallet, the device knows everything about the wallet: it holds the only key. In a multisig, it holds one key of three and has to trust the other two public keys it is told about. If malware on your computer or phone can swap one of those public keys, it can make "your" multisig addresses belong partly to the attacker, or make "change" go somewhere you do not control. BitBox's engineers described these attacks in detail in how nearly all personal hardware wallet multisig setups are insecure, and several vendors improved their firmware afterwards.

The features below are what close those gaps.

1. The script types you plan to use

Check that the device signs the multisig script your wallet uses. Native segwit multisig (P2WSH, usually on BIP 48 paths) is the most widely supported. Taproot multisig and miniscript policies (timelocks, heir paths) are supported by fewer devices. If you want a timelocked recovery path, confirm support first.

2. Wallet registration

Registration means the device is shown the whole multisig wallet once (all public keys, the threshold, the script type), you approve it on the device's screen, and the device remembers it (or a proof of it). After that:

  • it can show you receive addresses and confirm they belong to this wallet;
  • it can recognise change going back to the same wallet, and show it as change rather than as a payment;
  • a swapped public key produces a different wallet, which the device does not recognise.

Some devices store the wallet; others keep a short proof that the host sends back each time, as Ledger's Bitcoin app does with an HMAC. Some devices are stateless and rely on the details sent with each request. Ask how a device without registration verifies your cosigners and your change.

The BSMS standard (BIP 129) and output descriptors (BIP 380) are common ways to hand a wallet to a device.

3. Address verification on the device's screen

Before receiving a large amount, show the address on the hardware wallet and compare it with what your phone or computer shows. If malware changed the address on the computer's screen, the device's screen will not match. Look for:

  • the full address on screen, not a shortened one;
  • a check that the address belongs to the registered multisig, not just that it contains the device's own key;
  • for best protection, the same address shown on two different devices.

4. Clear payment review

When you sign, the device should show every output's address and amount, the fee, and which outputs are change. If it cannot recognise change, it will show change as a payment to an address you cannot check by eye, and you lose the ability to spot a swap.

5. PSBT support and how it connects

Multisig transactions travel between signers as PSBTs (BIP 174). How the PSBT reaches the device is a trade-off:

ConnectionStrengthsTrade-offs
USBSimple, fastNeeds a cable and a compatible port
BluetoothWorks with phonesA wireless link to secure and pair
QR codesAir-gapped, phone-friendlyLarge transactions need animated QR codes
NFCTap to send, no cablePhone support varies (iPhone apps need extra permissions)
microSD cardAir-gapped, any sizeSlow; files can linger on cards and computers

None is "the secure one". What matters is that the device shows and checks everything itself, whatever the channel.

6. Message signing at multisig paths

Some multisig wallets use the hardware wallet for more than payments: to approve a rule change, pair with a co-signer or prove ownership. They do it by asking the device to sign a short text with a key it controls, typically as a BIP 137-style signed message (or the newer BIP 322).

If a wallet you plan to use needs this, check three things:

  • Which key paths the device will sign a message with. Some firmware only signs messages with single-key paths, or refuses multisig account paths.
  • How much text it shows. A device that cuts the text after a fixed number of characters may hide the part you need to read.
  • That it shows the text at all. A device that signs a message without displaying it is signing blind.

7. Protection against malicious firmware

A device with tampered firmware could, in theory, leak its key through the random values in its signatures. Some devices (for example the BitBox02 and Blockstream's Jade) support an anti-exfil or anti-klepto protocol in which the phone or computer contributes randomness and checks that the device used it. Also worth weighing: open-source firmware, reproducible builds, and how firmware updates are verified.

8. Mixing brands

In a multisig, using devices from different vendors means one vendor's bug or supply-chain problem affects only one key. The cost is learning two or three interfaces. Many people consider it worth it.

A short checklist

  • Does it sign my wallet's script type?
  • Can I register the multisig and approve it on the device?
  • Does it show full receive addresses and confirm they belong to the registered wallet?
  • Does it recognise change?
  • How does it connect to the phone or computer I will use?
  • If my wallet needs message signing, will it sign at the paths it needs, and show the whole text?
  • Is the firmware open source and reproducible?

How Trikey approaches it

In Trikey, the hardware wallet is key 1: it approves payments over your daily limit, every loosening of the rules, pairing with the guardian, and recovery access for a new phone. That puts more weight on the features above than a plain multisig does. From the design document's hardware wallets by feature:

  • Script: plain wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) on BIP 48 paths, chosen because every major device can co-sign it.
  • Registration and address check: the wallet is registered on devices that need it (Ledger, BitBox02, Jade, Coldcard), and the vault's first address is shown on the device for you to compare, for every device.
  • Approvals are signed messages (BIP 137) of at most 240 characters, which show the new rules in clear, so you read them on the device's screen. Texts that name your alert contacts are kept within what the Jade displays before it truncates.
  • Connections: Ledger over Bluetooth; Trezor through Trezor Suite Lite; Jade by QR or Bluetooth; BitBox02 over USB-C on Android (the Nova also over Bluetooth); Coldcard Q by QR, and Coldcard Mk4 or Q over NFC; Keystone 3, Passport Prime and Specter DIY by QR; Passport (2nd generation) and Krux by QR for payments and microSD for signed messages.
  • SeedSigner signs payments but refuses messages at the multisig path Trikey's approvals use, so it works for payments and Recovery Key mode, not as the hardware wallet of a guardian wallet.
  • Anti-klepto is used with the BitBox02 for payments and most texts.

The most important caveat: only the Ledger has been tested on real hardware so far. Support for every other device was written from its firmware's source code and official clients and is untested on devices. If you own one, a hardware wallet test report on a test network is one of the most useful things you can contribute, even if everything works; the testers guide explains how to set up.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet, use only an amount you can afford to lose.

FAQ

Can I use any hardware wallet in a multisig?

Most current devices can sign standard P2WSH multisig. Whether they can register the wallet, verify addresses and recognise change varies, and those are what protect you.

Do I need three hardware wallets for a 2-of-3?

No. Many setups use one or two hardware wallets plus a phone key or a co-signing service. What matters is that the keys live in different places and no single device or place holds two.

Is an air-gapped hardware wallet safer for multisig?

Air-gapping removes a cable or wireless link, but the main protection in multisig is what the device verifies and shows. An air-gapped device that cannot recognise change is weaker than a connected one that can.

Why does my hardware wallet show a "register wallet" screen?

It is asking you to approve the multisig wallet's keys once. Compare what it shows with your wallet software (and ideally your other devices) before approving.

What does message signing have to do with multisig?

Nothing for payments. Some wallets use signed messages to let the hardware wallet approve non-payment actions, such as changing a spending limit. If yours does, the device must sign at the right path and show the whole text.

item.title: Collaborative Custody Compared: Who Holds the Third Key?
item.description: Bitkey, Casa, Unchained, Nunchuk and DIY multisig compared fairly: who holds which key, what each key can do, and what happens if a company goes away.
item.content:encoded:
"Collaborative custody" means a 2-of-3 multisig wallet in which you hold two keys and a company holds the third. It sits between handing your bitcoin to an exchange and carrying every key alone. Several good products work this way, and they differ in what the company's key is allowed to do. This article compares the main models by the question that matters most: who holds the third key, and what can that key do? It is written to be fair: each model has real strengths, and the right choice depends on what you want help with.

Product details change. Everything below is taken from each provider's public documentation as of November 2026; check their current pages before deciding.

The four models

1. An exchange or custodian holds everything

The simplest option: the company holds the keys, and you hold an account. Recovery is a password reset. The trade-off is that the bitcoin is the company's to move, freeze or lose, and your access depends on its solvency and its policies. Not self-custody, but worth naming as the baseline.

2. You hold one key (single-sig)

One hardware wallet and one seed phrase. Fully yours, simple and cheap, and every company could disappear without effect. The risk is that the seed is a single point of failure for both loss and theft (see what happens if you lose a key).

3. You hold two keys, a company holds one

The collaborative model. No party can spend alone: not you with one key, not the company with its key. What the company's key does varies:

  • A recovery key. The company signs only to help you after you lose a key. Day to day, you spend with your own two keys.
  • A co-signing key with rules. The company's server co-signs everyday payments from your phone, within limits, so you do not need your hardware wallet for small amounts. It also runs a delayed recovery.

4. You hold all three keys

Do-it-yourself multisig with a coordinator such as Sparrow, Nunchuk, Specter or Electrum, and three hardware wallets or seeds kept in different places. No company in the loop at all. The trade-off is that you are your own support desk, and everyday spending means fetching two devices.

The providers, briefly

Bitkey (Block)

A 2-of-3 with three fixed roles: an app key on your phone, Bitkey's own hardware device, and a server key held by Block. Block's server co-signs with your phone up to a daily limit you set, so small payments do not need the hardware. Over the limit, the hardware device signs. If you lose a key, Delay + Notify recovers it after a seven-day waiting period with alerts, and you can cancel a recovery you did not start. An Emergency Exit Kit lets you move your funds with your phone key and hardware key without Block's servers. The roles are fixed: you cannot swap in another hardware wallet or a different cosigner.

Good fit for: people who want everyday phone payments with a hardware backstop and a company that runs the server.

Casa

A 3-key vault (2-of-3) in which you hold a mobile key and a hardware key, and Casa holds the Casa Recovery Key. Casa's documentation says it holds only that key and cannot move funds with it alone; it exists to help you recover when you lose access to one of your keys. Casa also documents recovering without Casa (for example in Sparrow) and offers larger vaults and inheritance services.

Good fit for: people who want a guided setup, a recovery partner and support, with day-to-day spending on their own keys.

Unchained

A 2-of-3 vault in which you hold two keys (usually two hardware wallets) and Unchained holds one. Unchained's key acts as a backup and recovery key. Its help pages describe external recovery: spending from the vault with your two hardware wallets, the wallet configuration file and another multisig wallet (Caravan or Sparrow), without the Unchained platform. It also offers larger quorums, inheritance and financial services built around the vault.

Good fit for: larger holdings, people who want a long-term custody partner and an established company behind it.

Nunchuk

A wallet app that does both: fully self-managed multisig (every key yours) and assisted wallets, in which Nunchuk holds a Platform Key. Its documentation describes using that key for day-to-day co-signing and spending limits, on paid plans. It also offers inheritance planning.

Good fit for: people who want one app that can start self-managed and add a company key later.

Side by side

ExchangeSingle-sigCompany holds 1 of 3You hold 3 of 3
Who can spend aloneThe companyYouNobodyNobody
A single lost keyAccount resetFunds at risk without backupRecover with the other twoRecover with the other two
Phone-only everyday paymentsYesDepends on the walletWith a co-signing service (Bitkey, Nunchuk assisted)Not usually
Help when things go wrongSupport deskNoneSupport deskNone, or a friend
If the company disappearsDepends on the companyNothing changesYou still hold two keys; keep the wallet configurationNothing changes
What the company seesEverythingNothingUsually your wallet's addresses and transactionsNothing

What a company key gives you, honestly

  • Someone to call. Setup help, a recovery process and, for families, an inheritance process.
  • An always-on co-signer for phone payments, without running any hardware yourself.
  • Accountability. A company with a reputation and a legal identity.

What it costs

  • Fees. Most collaborative plans are subscriptions.
  • Dependence for what the key does. If the company stops, its features stop; your two keys still recover, as long as you kept the wallet configuration.
  • Privacy. A co-signer that checks your payments must see them, and usually knows your whole wallet.
  • Fixed choices. Some products fix the hardware or the roles; others let you choose.

None of these is a flaw in a particular company. They are the shape of the model.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey keeps the everyday shape of the co-signing model, phone payments within a daily limit and a waiting-period recovery with alerts, and gives the third key back to you. The co-signer, the Trikey Guardian, is an app on your own home server (Umbrel, Start9, or a computer or NAS running Docker). The design document says it plainly: no company runs a server, a guardian or a cosigner for anyone.

  • Key 1: a hardware wallet of your choice (Ledger, Trezor, Coldcard, Jade, BitBox02, Keystone, Passport, Krux or Specter DIY), not one brand.
  • Key 2: your phone. With the guardian, it pays within your daily limit.
  • Key 3: your guardian, which co-signs only within the rules your hardware wallet approved, and runs a 7, 14 or 30-day Delay & Notify recovery.
  • Recover anywhere: a plain wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) descriptor, so any multisig wallet can move the coins with two of your keys.

What you give up compared with a company: there is no support desk, you keep a home server running, and if it goes offline, phone-only payments wait (your phone and hardware wallet still move any amount). A remote compromise of your home server gives up one key of three, the same exposure as a company's co-signing server being breached (threat model). And unlike the products above, Trikey is not a finished product.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide explains how to try it. Trikey is an independent open-source project and is not affiliated with any of the companies named here.

FAQ

What is the best Bitkey alternative?

It depends on what you like about Bitkey. For a company-run co-signer with phone payments, look at assisted multisig such as Nunchuk's. For a recovery partner with your own two keys, Casa or Unchained. For no company at all, do-it-yourself multisig, or a self-hosted co-signer such as Trikey once it is ready.

Can the company in collaborative custody take my bitcoin?

Not alone: it holds one key of three, and the wallet needs two. It could refuse to sign, which is why you should always be able to spend with your own two keys.

What happens to my funds if the company shuts down?

You still hold two keys. With the wallet's configuration (descriptor) and any multisig wallet, you can move the funds. Save that file today and test it once.

Is collaborative custody still self-custody?

Most people count it as such, because no single party, the company included, can move the funds. You hold the majority of the keys.

item.title: A Bitcoin Co-Signer on Your Home Server: What It Protects
item.description: What running a bitcoin node and a co-signing key on Umbrel, Start9 or Docker protects against, what it does not, and how to run one safely at home.
item.content:encoded:
Home servers such as Umbrel and Start9 made it easy to run a Bitcoin node in a box on a shelf. Most people use one to check their own transactions and keep their addresses private. A newer idea goes one step further: let the box hold one key of a 2-of-3 multisig wallet and co-sign payments under rules you set, the way a company's server does in collaborative custody. This article explains what a home node protects, what a home co-signer adds, what neither protects against, and how to run one without creating new risks.

What your own node already gives you

You check the chain yourself

A wallet has to learn which coins you own and whether a payment confirmed. Without a node, it asks someone else's server, and trusts the answer. With your own node, your wallet asks software you run, which has checked every block itself.

Your addresses stay private

Most mobile and desktop wallets look up addresses through an Electrum server. A public one learns every address you ask about, and usually your IP address too, so it can link your whole wallet together. Umbrel and Start9 offer Electrum server apps (such as Electrs or Fulcrum) that run next to Bitcoin Core, so your wallet can ask your own box instead.

You broadcast your own transactions

Sending through your own node means no third party sees a payment before the network does.

What a node does not do on its own: hold keys or enforce any rule about spending. That is the co-signer's job.

What a co-signer on the box adds

A co-signer is a key that signs only when a request meets its rules. Companies run them for collaborative custody (see collaborative custody compared). Running one at home gives you the same kinds of rules without a company holding a key:

  • A spending limit. Your phone plus the co-signer can pay up to a daily amount. Above it, the hardware wallet must sign. A stolen phone is worth at most the limit.
  • A waiting period for recovery. If you lose a key, the co-signer helps you recover, but only after a delay with alerts (see Delay & Notify).
  • Rules that only a stronger key can loosen. Raising the limit or shortening the delay needs the hardware wallet, not just the phone.
  • Alerts to you and people you trust when something unusual happens.

A few open-source projects explore self-hosted co-signers with policies, such as Ledger's resigner and Coinkite's CKBunker; check each project's repository for its status and intended use.

What it does not protect against

Being honest about the limits is the most useful part of this article.

A compromised box is one key of three

If someone takes over your home server remotely, they hold the co-signer's key. In a 2-of-3 wallet that is one key: not enough to spend. It is the same exposure as a company's co-signing server being breached. But it means the co-signer must never be your only line of defence: someone holding the box and one of your other keys holds two keys.

Burglary

A burglar who takes your phone and your home server has two of your three devices. If they keep the box running and its rules hold, that buys them the daily limit, and any recovery they start sets off the alerts. If they unplug it, a good design makes the server lock itself on restart (a key encrypted on disk is useless without its passphrase), so the box is worthless. Either way, keep your hardware wallet's seed words outside your home: the hardware wallet plus the phone would be a pair with no limit.

Downtime

Power cuts, internet outages, a failed disk or an update gone wrong all stop the co-signer. A design worth trusting keeps your money reachable without it: in a 2-of-3, your phone and hardware wallet are still a spending pair.

Other apps on the same box

App platforms run many containers side by side. Treat every other app as a neighbour that might be compromised: the co-signer should not trust requests just because they come from the local network, and its web page should sit behind the platform's login.

Backups that copy the key

Automatic backups of a server can quietly create extra copies of the co-signer's key, and restoring an old copy can roll back its records (for example, how much of today's limit was used). For a key that is one of three, "no backup, replace it if lost" is often the safer rule: the other two keys move the coins to a new wallet with a new co-signer.

Running one safely

  • Open no ports. Port forwarding exposes the box to the whole internet. Prefer designs that only connect outwards (through relays or Tor) and reach the box's web page through the platform's own login, a VPN such as Tailscale, or an HTTPS proxy.
  • Use a strong, unique passphrase for the co-signer's key, and know where it is written.
  • Keep the node's own wallet empty. Apps on the box often get broad access to Bitcoin Core's RPC. If the node holds a wallet with funds, an app that is taken over could use it. Where you can, give each app a restricted RPC user with Bitcoin Core's rpcauth and rpcwhitelist settings.
  • Send alerts somewhere a phone thief cannot reach: a second device, a family member, an email account.
  • Plan for the box dying. Write down how you would move the coins with your other two keys, and try it once on a test network.
  • Keep it physically modest. A small box on a shelf, on a UPS if power is unreliable, not advertised to visitors.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey's key 3 is the Trikey Guardian, an app for your own home server: an Umbrel (through a community app store), a Start9 (a package you build yourself for now), or any Mac, PC, Linux machine or NAS with Docker. From the design document's components and threat model:

  • It reads the chain from your own node by default (the box's Electrs on Umbrel and Start9), or from Bitcoin Core alone. A public Electrum server is possible for people without a node, behind a warning: it would see the wallet's addresses and could hide coins, but never spend or change a rule.
  • It opens no port at home. The phone and the guardian talk through nostr relays, both connecting outwards, with messages end-to-end encrypted (NIP-44) inside gift wraps (NIP-59). Relays see ciphertext and metadata; they can drop a message, not read or forge one.
  • Key 3 lives in memory only while unlocked. On disk it is encrypted under your passphrase (Argon2id). After any restart the guardian is locked until you unlock it with the passphrase, or, if you turn it on, with a confirmation on your hardware wallet.
  • The platforms' backups leave the guardian out, on purpose, for the reasons above. If the box dies, your phone and hardware wallet move the coins to a new wallet with a fresh guardian ("Replace guardian").
  • A one-time setup code protects the first run, so another app on the box cannot set up the guardian before you do.
  • Its rules: phone payments within a rolling 24-hour limit, a 7, 14 or 30-day Delay & Notify recovery, and any loosening only with a hardware wallet approval.
  • Alerts go beyond nostr if you want: email through your own account, ntfy, a webhook or Telegram, and they still go out while the guardian is locked.

The design is explicit about the limit: a remote compromise of the home server gives up one key of three, and phone-only payments wait while the guardian is offline.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide shows how to install the guardian on Umbrel or Docker with a signet node, and the site has setup videos.

FAQ

Do I need my own node to use a hardware wallet?

No. But without one, your wallet trusts someone else's server for your balance and history, and that server learns your addresses.

Is it safe to keep a bitcoin key on an Umbrel or Start9?

As one key of a 2-of-3, with a passphrase-encrypted key, no open ports and the other keys elsewhere, it is a reasonable design. As your only key, or as two keys of three, it is not.

What happens if my home server is hacked?

The attacker holds one key of three and cannot spend alone. Move the coins to a new wallet with your other two keys and set up a fresh co-signer.

What if my internet or power goes down?

The co-signer stops answering. In a 2-of-3 your other two keys can still spend; the everyday shortcut waits until the box is back.

Does a home co-signer need port forwarding?

It should not. Designs that connect outwards only, through relays or Tor, avoid exposing your home network.

item.title: Delay & Notify: Why Bitcoin Recovery Should Wait
item.description: Why a waiting period with alerts is the safest way to recover a bitcoin wallet with one key, and how cosigner delays compare with on-chain timelocks.
item.content:encoded:
Any wallet that lets you recover with fewer keys than usual has a problem: whatever lets you in after a loss would also let a thief in. A waiting period solves this in a simple way. The recovery is allowed, but it takes days, and everyone who should know is told every day. The real owner, who lost a key, can afford to wait. A thief cannot wait unnoticed. This article explains why that works, the two ways a waiting period can be enforced (by a cosigner, or by Bitcoin's own timelocks), and how to choose its length.

The recovery dilemma

In a 2-of-3 multisig wallet, two keys spend. If you lose one key, the other two are enough. But some setups want more than that: a way to recover when only one of your own keys survives, with help from a third party or a server that holds the third key.

That help is dangerous if it is instant. Whoever steals your one remaining key, or tricks the helper, would get the same instant recovery. Asking security questions or sending an email code does not settle who is the owner; both can be phished or guessed.

Time can. A legitimate recovery is rarely urgent by the hour. A theft almost always is: the attacker wants the coins before you notice. So a recovery that waits, and announces itself loudly while it waits, turns the attacker's need for speed against them.

What "Delay & Notify" means

The name comes from Bitkey, which uses it for recovering a lost key. The pattern has three parts:

  1. Delay. A recovery started with one key does not complete until a fixed period has passed. Bitkey's support pages describe a seven-day delay.
  2. Notify. During the delay, the owner is alerted, ideally on several channels and devices, including ones the attacker does not hold.
  3. Cancel. Anyone legitimately alerted can stop the recovery before it completes.

At the end of the delay, the funds move to a new wallet with a replacement key. They do not simply unlock.

Two ways to enforce a waiting period

A cosigner that follows rules

One of the keys is held by a cosigner (a company's server, or a server you run) that signs a recovery only after the delay has passed and nobody cancelled. This is how Bitkey's Delay + Notify works, with Block's server holding one of the three keys.

Strengths: the delay can be cancelled, alerts are built in, rules can be changed later, and it works with any hardware wallet because the Bitcoin script is an ordinary multisig.

Limits: the delay is enforced by software, not by Bitcoin. If the cosigner is compromised and an attacker holds one of your keys, they have two keys and can skip the delay. The cosigner also has to be online and honest about time, so a good design checks the clock against the blockchain rather than trusting the server's clock alone.

Timelocks in the Bitcoin script

Bitcoin can enforce time itself:

  • Absolute timelocks make a transaction or a script path valid only after a given block height or date (BIP 65, OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY).
  • Relative timelocks make a path valid only after a coin has been confirmed for a given number of blocks or amount of time (BIP 68 and BIP 112, OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY).

Wallets built on miniscript, such as Liana, use these to add a recovery path: your normal keys spend at any time, and a recovery key (or an heir's key) can spend only after the coins have sat unmoved for, say, a year.

Strengths: no server is needed, and nobody can shorten the wait, not even with every server compromised.

Limits: a relative timelock counts from when each coin was confirmed, so you must move ("refresh") your coins before the timer runs out, or the recovery path becomes spendable. There is no cancel button: you "cancel" by spending the coins to a new address. Alerts are not built in; someone has to watch the chain. And fewer hardware wallets can sign these scripts than plain multisig.

Covenants: not available yet

Covenant proposals would let coins themselves enforce "wait, and allow a cancel to a safe address" on-chain. The best known, OP_VAULT (BIP 345), is marked Closed in the BIP repository. Any such proposal would need a soft fork, and none is active on Bitcoin, so no wallet can use one today.

Side by side

Cosigner-enforced delayScript timelock (miniscript)
Who enforces the waitThe cosigner's softwareEvery Bitcoin node
Can a recovery be cancelled?Yes, by anyone alertedOnly by moving the coins first
AlertsBuilt inNeed a separate watcher
Coins need refreshingNoYes, before each timelock expires
Hardware wallet supportAny device that signs multisigFewer devices
Bypassed byCosigner compromise plus one stolen keyTheft of the keys in the normal spending path

Neither is strictly better. A cosigner delay is flexible and loud; a script timelock is strict and quiet.

Choosing the length

  • Longer gives you time to notice while travelling, ill or offline, and gives your contacts time to reach you.
  • Shorter gets you back to your money sooner after a genuine loss.

A week is a common floor. Thirty days suits people who are often out of reach. Whatever you choose, the wait only protects you if the alerts reach someone: send them to more than one device and at least one person you trust, through channels a phone thief does not control.

Two failure modes worth knowing

Phishing that imitates an alert. A fake "recovery started, click here to cancel" message is an obvious attack. Real alerts should never need you to click a link or sign in. If a wallet's alerts never contain links, any message with one is fake.

Contested recovery. If a thief holds one of your keys and you hold another, each can cancel the other's recovery. The result is a stalemate: the funds are frozen, not stolen. That is the price of letting any key holder cancel. You get out by finding a second key (a backup) or by outlasting the thief.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey uses a cosigner-enforced Delay & Notify, with one difference from Bitkey: the cosigner, the Trikey Guardian, runs on your own home server, so no company holds a key or decides on a recovery. From the design document's rules the guardian enforces:

  • You pick the delay: 7, 14 or 30 days.
  • Starting a recovery pauses phone-only payments, so a phone thief who starts one gains nothing in the meantime.
  • Alerts go out every day as end-to-end encrypted nostr messages to your devices and your alert contacts, and optionally by email, ntfy, a webhook or Telegram. On mainnet the guardian requires at least one alert contact.
  • Any of them can cancel. A cancel from someone other than the person who started the recovery keeps phone payments paused until the hardware wallet resumes them.
  • Three clocks must agree before the guardian co-signs: the system clock, the blockchain's median time past, and the number of blocks mined since the start. A tampered clock cannot shorten the wait.
  • Alerts never carry a link or a button and never ask anyone to sign in.
  • A fee cap stops a recovery from burning the funds in fees, and the funds move to a new 2-of-3 wallet.

The honest limit is the one above: if someone took over your home server and held one of your other keys, they would hold two keys of three. The threat model goes through this and the other cases, including the contested stalemate.

Trikey also uses Bitcoin's own timelocks, in its Recovery Key mode for people without a home server: the phone's small spending balance is refilled by a chain of pre-signed refills, each of which can confirm only 1,008 blocks (about a week) after the one before it (a BIP 68 relative timelock), so even a phone thief holding every refill gets at most one per period. Recovery in that mode needs any two keys and has no waiting period. Recovery Key mode is for test networks only.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide suggests starting a recovery as if you had lost your phone and letting it run in the background.

FAQ

Why can't recovery be instant if I can prove who I am?

Because anything that proves your identity online (an email, a code, an answer to a question) can be stolen or faked. Time and alerts to several people are much harder to fake.

What happens if I miss the alerts?

The recovery completes at the end of the delay. That is why alerts should reach more than one device and at least one other person, and why a longer delay suits people who are often offline.

Can a thief cancel my genuine recovery?

If they hold one of your keys, yes, and you can cancel theirs. Neither side can take the funds; they stay frozen until one side gives up or you restore a second key.

Do timelocks work on any hardware wallet?

Plain multisig works almost everywhere. Script paths with timelocks need devices that can sign those scripts, which is a shorter list. Check before you commit to a design. See choosing a hardware wallet for multisig.

item.title: 2-of-3 Multisig Explained: How It Works and What It Costs
item.description: How 2-of-3 bitcoin multisig works, what each pair of keys is for, how it compares with single-sig, and the real costs: fees, backups and complexity.
item.content:encoded:
A 2-of-3 multisig wallet holds bitcoin behind three keys and lets any two of them spend. Lose one key and the other two still move your money. Have one key stolen and the thief still cannot spend. That is the whole idea, and it is enforced by Bitcoin itself, not by a company or an app. This article explains how it works under the hood, what each pair of keys is good for, how it compares with an ordinary single-key wallet, and what it costs you in fees, backups and care.

What "2-of-3" means

A normal bitcoin wallet has one private key (in practice, one seed phrase that produces many keys). Whoever holds that seed can spend. This is called single-sig: one signature is enough.

A multisig wallet replaces that single key with a rule: M signatures out of N possible keys. In a 2-of-3 wallet there are three keys, usually kept on three different devices or in three different places, and any two of them must sign before coins can move. The three keys are equal: no key is "the main one" as far as Bitcoin is concerned.

The rule is part of the coins themselves. When you receive bitcoin to a multisig address, the address commits to a script that says "two valid signatures from these three public keys". Every node on the network checks that rule before accepting a spend. No server can waive it, and no single key can break it.

How a 2-of-3 wallet works under the hood

You do not need these details to use multisig, but they explain the backup advice later on.

Three extended public keys

Each of the three devices holds its own seed and exports an extended public key (an xpub) for a multisig account. A common standard for the account path is BIP 48, for example m/48'/0'/0'/2' for a native segwit multisig account on mainnet. The xpub lets the wallet derive public keys but not spend.

One address per index, from all three keys

For each new receive address, the wallet takes the next public key from each of the three xpubs and builds a script that requires two signatures from those three keys. Today that script is usually wrapped as a P2WSH (native segwit) output, so the address starts with bc1q and is longer than a single-sig one.

The descriptor ties it together

The full recipe for the wallet, "2 of these three xpubs, at these paths, in a P2WSH script", is written as an output descriptor. For a 2-of-3 it looks like this (shortened):

wsh(sortedmulti(2,[f00d1234/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6E.../0/*,[ab12cd34/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6F.../0/*,[99887766/48h/0h/0h/2h]xpub6D.../0/*))

wsh is the P2WSH wrapper, sortedmulti(2, …) means "two of these keys, sorted into a fixed order", and each bracket names the device fingerprint and path a key came from. Descriptors are standardised in BIP 380 and BIP 383, and Bitcoin Core documents them in its descriptors guide. The descriptor holds no secret, but it is essential: without the other keys' xpubs, your seed alone cannot find your coins.

Signing passes a PSBT around

To spend, one device creates a Partially Signed Bitcoin Transaction (BIP 174), signs it, and hands it to a second device, which adds its signature. Once two signatures are in, the transaction is complete and can be broadcast. The PSBT can travel over USB, Bluetooth, a QR code, an SD card or a network message; the signatures are what matter.

What each pair of keys is for

Because any two keys spend, a 2-of-3 setup gives you three different pairs. Good designs give each pair a job:

  • Everyday pair. Two keys that are easy to reach together, for routine spending.
  • Big-decision pair. A pair that includes a key kept offline, for large payments or for changing how the wallet behaves.
  • Recovery pair. The two keys you still have when one is lost or stolen. They move everything to a new wallet with a fresh third key.

The important property: no single key can spend, and no single loss locks you out. Both of those are true at the same time, which a single-key wallet cannot offer.

Single-sig vs 2-of-3: what you are trading

People ask whether multisig is "worth it". The honest answer is that it changes which risks you carry rather than removing risk.

Single-sig (one seed)2-of-3 multisig
One key lostFunds lost unless the seed backup existsStill spendable with the other two
One key stolen or seed photographedThief can spend everythingThief cannot spend alone
Backups to keepOne seed (plus passphrase, if used)Each key's backup plus the descriptor
Transaction size and feesSmallestLarger inputs: two signatures and the script
On-chain privacyLooks like most walletsA spend reveals a 2-of-3 script
Setup and recovery effortLowHigher: registration, address checks, more steps

A single seed is a single point of failure in both directions: it can be lost, and it can be found. Adding a BIP 39 passphrase spreads that risk across two items, but whoever learns both still holds a complete key, and losing the passphrase loses the funds.

Multisig removes the single point of failure but adds moving parts. If you store two of the three keys in the same drawer, you are back to one point of failure, with more complexity. If you lose the descriptor and one key, recovery can become very hard.

For a small amount you spend often, a well-backed-up single-sig wallet is a reasonable choice. As the amount grows, or if theft or a single mistake worries you more than complexity does, 2-of-3 starts to pay for itself.

What multisig does not fix

  • Two keys in one place. A burglar who finds two keys in the same house holds a spending pair.
  • Coercion. If someone can force you to use two keys, multisig alone does not stop them. Waiting periods and limits help more here (see Delay & Notify: why recovery should wait).
  • Signing the wrong thing. If malware swaps the destination address and you approve it on both devices without reading the screen, the payment goes out. Devices that show the address you are paying, and the wallet's own change, are what protect you (see choosing a hardware wallet for multisig).
  • Lost metadata. Without the descriptor (or all the xpubs), the keys you hold may not be enough to find the coins.

2-of-3 or 3-of-5?

Larger setups such as 3-of-5 tolerate two lost keys and make theft harder, but every payment needs three devices and every recovery more coordination. For an individual, 2-of-3 is the common middle ground: one loss is survivable, one theft is harmless, and only two devices are needed to sign.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey is an open-source 2-of-3 wallet in which you hold all three keys, and each pair has one job:

  • Key 1, any hardware wallet (Ledger, Trezor, Coldcard, Jade, BitBox02 and others), kept in a drawer.
  • Key 2, your phone, behind its biometrics.
  • Key 3, the Trikey Guardian, an app on your own home server (Umbrel, Start9 or plain Docker).

Phone plus guardian is the everyday pair: the guardian co-signs phone payments only within a daily limit you set. Phone plus hardware wallet is the big-decision pair: larger payments and any loosening of the rules. Hardware wallet plus guardian is the recovery pair for a lost phone, behind a waiting period with daily alerts.

Under the hood every Trikey wallet is a plain wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) descriptor on BIP 48 paths, the same kind of script shown above. That choice is deliberate: it is the multisig script every major hardware wallet can co-sign, and it means any multisig-capable wallet can recover the coins with two of your keys, without Trikey. The reasons, and what was left out (taproot multisig, miniscript, MuSig2), are in the design document's decisions.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet anyway, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide explains how to try it.

FAQ

Is 2-of-3 multisig safer than a single hardware wallet?

It removes the single point of failure: one lost or stolen key no longer decides the outcome. It is only safer if you keep the three keys apart and back up the descriptor. Done carelessly, it adds ways to make mistakes.

Can I recover a multisig wallet with just the seed words?

Usually not with two seeds alone. You also need the third key's xpub, which is in the descriptor. Keep a copy of the descriptor with each key backup; it reveals your balance and history to whoever reads it, but it cannot spend. More in bitcoin inheritance without a company.

Does multisig cost more in fees?

Yes. Each multisig input carries two signatures and the script, so it is larger than a single-sig input and costs more to spend. Fewer, larger coins keep the difference small.

Can I mix hardware wallet brands in one multisig?

Yes, and many people do, so that one vendor's bug does not affect every key. Each device must support the script type and, ideally, let you register the wallet and check addresses on its screen.

How is multisig different from splitting a seed (Shamir or SLIP-39)?

A split seed is still one key: the shares are combined into the full seed when you need it, at which point it exists in one place. Multisig keeps the keys separate forever; each device signs on its own and no device ever holds the others' keys.

item.title: worse_query: What an iOS Bug Can Take From Your Wallet
item.description: An iOS bug lets malicious apps read other apps' files. What that exposes in a bitcoin wallet, what it doesn't, and what to do today.
item.content:encoded:
On 10 November 2026, Binance warned iPhone users about worse_query, a bug in iOS that lets a malicious app read files that belong to other apps. Binance named seed phrases, private keys and login credentials as being at risk "across the entire ecosystem" (Bitcoin Magazine). That is alarming for anyone with a wallet on their phone. But what a bug like this can take depends on one thing: where your wallet keeps its keys. This post explains that, so you can judge your own wallet, and lists what to do today.

What worse_query is, as reported so far

These are the facts as reported on 10 November 2026. Check the latest news before you act on them.

  • It is a sandbox escape. Every iPhone app is meant to live in its own sandbox: it can read its own files and nobody else's. worse_query breaks that wall, so an app you install can read files that another app wrote.
  • A researcher, forcequitOS, published it as a public proof of concept on 8 November. The security firm SlowMist lists iOS 26.0 to 26.7.2 and iOS 27.2 as affected; Binance's warning names 26.7.1, 27.0.1 and 27.2 (SlowMist on X, CryptoTicker). If your version sits between those, assume it is affected too.
  • Apple released iOS 27.2.1 and 26.7.3 on 9 November. SlowMist says 27.2.1 stops the bug, but Apple's security notes don't mention it, so treat the fix as likely, not confirmed (Security Affairs).
  • No attack or theft had been reported when this was written.
  • SlowMist's point is the one that matters here: the bug alone doesn't steal anything. The risk is an untrusted app on your phone, combined with a wallet that keeps seeds, keystores or caches in plain files.
  • The attacker needs an app on your phone. It is not a remote attack: someone has to get you to install a malicious app, most likely from outside the App Store (a "sideloaded" or manually signed app).

Files and the Keychain are two different places

A phone wallet can keep its secrets in two kinds of storage, and worse_query reaches only one of them.

  1. The app's own files. A database, settings, caches. These live in the app's folder, and the sandbox is the only thing that protects them from other apps. A sandbox escape like worse_query reads them.
  2. The Keychain (on Android, the Keystore). It is a system service, not a file in the app's folder. Its items are encrypted with keys guarded by the phone's secure chip (the Secure Enclave on iPhone). An item can also be set to need Face ID or a fingerprint every time it is read, and to never leave the device. A bug that only reads files doesn't hand over what is in the Keychain.

So the question for any wallet is: does it write the seed, or a private key, into its own files? A wallet that keeps them in the Keychain loses privacy to a bug like this: your addresses, your balance, your history. A wallet that keeps a seed in a file, even "obfuscated", can lose the money.

How to find out for your wallet:

  • Look for a security page or a threat model in the wallet's documentation that says where keys are stored. For an open-source wallet you can also read the code.
  • Words to look for: Keychain, Secure Enclave, Android Keystore, "this device only", "biometric".
  • Be wary of wallets that never say. "Bank-grade encryption" doesn't tell you where the key is.

What a file-reading bug can expose

Even when the keys are safe, an app's files hold things you'd rather keep to yourself:

  • Your public keys and addresses. Many wallets store an extended public key (xpub) or a descriptor. With it, someone can list every address of the wallet, so your balance and your whole history. They can't spend with it, but it tells them what you hold, which matters for phishing and physical safety.
  • Labels and notes: what you called each payment and who you paid.
  • Session tokens for exchanges and other services, if an app keeps them in files. This is where "logins at risk" comes from.

What to do today

  1. Update iOS. Settings, General, Software Update. Take the newest version offered: 27.2.1 or later on iOS 27, 26.7.3 or later if your phone stays on iOS 26. On 27.1, 27.0.x or an older 26.x, update.

  2. Remove apps you don't trust, especially ones that didn't come from the App Store: sideloaded or manually signed apps from strangers, "modded" apps, cracked games. The bug needs one of those on your phone to do anything.

  3. Don't panic-move your coins into something new. Scammers follow security news: expect fake "migration tools", fake support accounts and "verify your wallet" messages. Nobody legitimate will ask for your seed words.

  4. If you have reason to think your phone was compromised (a strange app you installed, signs of tampering), treat its keys as exposed:

    • Create a new wallet on a clean, updated device.
    • Move the funds there.
    • Reset your exchange sessions and passwords.

    A restore of the same seed on a new phone isn't enough: whoever has a copy can still use it. Our post on losing a phone, a hardware wallet or a seed phrase goes through the cases.

Why a phone key shouldn't be the only key

worse_query is one bug. There will be others, in iOS, in Android, in apps. That is the strongest argument against keeping all your bitcoin behind one key on a phone. A phone runs hundreds of other apps and connects to everything; it is the most exposed device you own.

With 2-of-3 multisig, the phone's key is one of three, and moving money needs two. A phone bug, even one that did reach the key, would give an attacker one key. Pair that with a daily limit and an alert on the second key, and the worst case of a phone compromise becomes "at most one day's limit", not "everything".

Trikey and worse_query

Trikey is an open-source 2-of-3 wallet: your hardware wallet (key 1), your phone (key 2) and the Trikey Guardian on your own home server (key 3). How it stands against a file-reading bug:

  • Key 2 lives in the Keychain, set to "this device only", never in backups, and readable only with Face ID. Every other key the app holds is in the Keychain or Keystore too. The app's files hold the wallet's public descriptor, the guardian's pairing details, labels and history: a privacy loss if read, with no power to sign. The full list, item by item, is in what the phone app keeps, and where.
  • Even key 2 alone moves at most the daily limit. The guardian co-signs phone-only payments within a limit you set. Raising the limit, changing a rule or starting a recovery needs your hardware wallet, or waits through a Delay & Notify period that alerts you every day (rules the guardian enforces).
  • If you suspect your phone, you can lock the guardian from the phone or its web page, restore key 2 on a clean phone from your backup, and use "Replace guardian" to move your coins to a fresh wallet.
  • About "manually signed apps": while the iPhone app isn't on the App Store, testers build Trikey themselves from its public source code, which iOS counts as a manually signed app. Building an open-source app yourself is not what the warning is about. The warning is about apps from people you don't know. Keep your own build, update iOS, and remove anything you don't trust.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet anyway, use only an amount you can afford to lose.

FAQ

Is my seed phrase exposed by worse_query?

Only if your wallet writes it into its own files. Wallets that keep the seed in the iPhone Keychain, especially with Face ID required, are not exposed by a bug that only reads files. Check your wallet's documentation, update iOS, and remove apps you don't trust.

Do I need to move my bitcoin?

Not because of the news alone. Move it if you installed something you don't trust, or see signs your phone was tampered with. Then move it to a wallet created on a clean device, not to the same seed restored elsewhere.

Does a hardware wallet protect me?

Its keys never touch the phone, so a phone bug can't read them. What it can reveal is your xpub, if a companion app stores it: that is privacy, not access to the coins.

item.title: Lost Your Hardware Wallet, Phone or Seed Phrase?
item.description: What happens to your bitcoin if you lose a hardware wallet, a phone or a seed phrase, case by case, with the steps to take and the scams to avoid.
item.content:encoded:
Your bitcoin is not inside your hardware wallet or your phone. It sits on the blockchain, locked to keys, and a device is only a safe place to keep and use those keys. So what losing a device means depends on one question: do you still have another way to produce the same keys? This guide goes through the common cases, from a lost device with a good backup to a lost seed phrase, for single-key wallets and for multisig, and says what to do in each.

First, three rules that apply to every case

  1. Nobody can recover keys for you. No support desk, "recovery service" or website can bring back a lost seed phrase. People who search for help after a loss are a favourite target for scams: fake support numbers, paid "recovery" firms and pages that ask you to type your seed words. Never enter seed words on a website or give them to anyone.
  2. If a key may be in someone else's hands, move the coins. A backup lets you restore, but it does not make the lost copy harmless. When in doubt, send everything to a new wallet with fresh keys.
  3. Act on the backup you actually have. Check it before you need it: the words are legible, the order is right, and any passphrase is recorded somewhere you will find it.

Single-key wallets: case by case

You lost the hardware wallet but have the seed phrase

Your funds are safe. Restore the seed phrase on a new device (same brand or any other that supports the standard, usually BIP 39), add the passphrase if you used one, and check that your balance appears.

Then decide whether to move the coins. The lost device is protected by its PIN, and most devices wipe or permanently lock themselves after a number of wrong PINs, but you cannot know who has it or what they can try. If the amount matters, create a new wallet with a new seed, back it up, and send everything to it.

The device was stolen

Same steps, with more urgency. Restore from your seed on another device and move the funds to a fresh wallet before a thief has time to work on the PIN or the device.

You still have the device but lost the seed phrase

Nothing is lost yet, but you are one accident away from it. Do not wait:

  1. Set up a new wallet with a new seed and write that seed down carefully.
  2. Check the new backup (many devices offer a "verify backup" step).
  3. Send all funds from the old wallet to the new one.

Avoid trying to "recover" the old seed through software or online tools. A new, properly backed-up wallet is faster and safer.

Your seed phrase may have been seen

A photo in the cloud, a sheet left in a drawer that someone else opened, words typed into a website: treat the seed as compromised. Move everything to a new wallet with a new seed now. Restoring or "securing" the old seed does nothing.

You lost both the device and the seed phrase

If there is no other copy of the seed and no wallet file on an old computer, the coins cannot be moved by anyone. This is the hard edge of self-custody, and the main reason people move to setups with more than one key.

A phone wallet was lost or stolen

For a single-key wallet on a phone, the seed phrase backup is everything. If you have it, restore it on another device and move the funds to a new wallet: the old phone still holds a copy of the key, protected only by its screen lock and the app's own lock. Also lock or erase the phone remotely and secure the email and phone number accounts it was signed into.

Multisig wallets: losing one key is survivable

In a 2-of-3 multisig wallet any two keys spend, so losing one key is an inconvenience, not a loss.

The recovery routine

  1. Use the two keys you still have.
  2. Create a new wallet: the two surviving keys plus a fresh third key (often at a new account on the same devices).
  3. Send everything from the old wallet to the new one.
  4. Back up the new wallet's descriptor and the new key.

Why move instead of just replacing the lost device? The old wallet's rule includes the lost key forever. If someone finds that key, they hold one of the three. Moving to a new wallet takes it out of the picture.

What you need besides the keys

Two seeds alone are usually not enough to find the coins. Your wallet software also needs the descriptor: the three public keys and how they are combined. Keep a copy of it with each key backup. It holds no secret (it cannot spend), but it shows your balance and history to whoever reads it.

When two keys are lost

If two of three keys are gone, a 2-of-3 wallet is in the same position as a single-key wallet with no backup. Restore whatever seeds you have from their backups before you consider anything else.

Why some wallets make you wait

Some wallets let a single surviving key start a recovery, but only after a waiting period, with alerts sent to you during it. The point is to make a stolen key slow and noisy rather than fast and silent: if you did not start the recovery, you have days to cancel it. We cover this in Delay & Notify: why recovery should wait.

How Trikey approaches it

Trikey is a 2-of-3 wallet with a hardware wallet (key 1), your phone (key 2) and the Trikey Guardian on your own home server (key 3). Its recovery flows follow the cases above:

What you lostWhat happens in Trikey
Phone, with its backupRestore the phone key on a new phone from your encrypted backup file and recovery code. No waiting.
Phone, no backupThe hardware wallet lets a new phone reach the guardian, and a recovery starts. It waits 7, 14 or 30 days (your choice), alerts you and your alert contacts every day, and any of you can cancel it. Then the money moves to a new 2-of-3 wallet.
Phone stolenA thief with an unlocked phone can spend at most your daily limit. Raising the limit needs the hardware wallet. Starting a recovery pauses phone-only payments.
Hardware walletRestore its seed words on a new device, or use the phone and guardian to run the same waiting-period recovery.
Hardware wallet stolenIt is PIN-locked and one key of three. A recovery someone starts with it triggers the daily alerts, and you cancel it.
Home server dies or is stolenThe phone and hardware wallet still move any amount. "Replace guardian" moves the coins to a new wallet with a new guardian. The guardian keeps key 3 encrypted and locks itself after any restart, so an unplugged box is useless to a thief.

Because the wallet is a standard wsh(sortedmulti(2,…)) descriptor, any two of your keys can also move the coins in another multisig wallet, without Trikey.

The full table, including the cases where a thief and the owner each hold one key, is in the design document's recovery flows and threat model. The site's pick a key to lose section walks through it with short videos.

Status: Trikey is pre-alpha and has not been audited. Use it on test networks (signet, testnet4 or regtest); if you try mainnet, use only an amount you can afford to lose. The testers guide includes a step where you delete the app and restore from your backup, which is worth rehearsing with any wallet.

FAQ

Is my bitcoin gone if I lose my hardware wallet?

No, not if you have the seed phrase (and passphrase, if you used one). Restore it on a new device. Consider moving the funds to a fresh wallet afterwards.

Can the manufacturer recover my wallet?

No. Hardware wallet makers do not have your seed. Anyone claiming to recover a wallet for a fee, or asking for your seed words, should be treated as a scam.

I forgot my PIN but have the seed. What now?

Most devices wipe or lock themselves after too many wrong attempts, and many let you reset them. Either way, restore from the seed phrase on the reset device or a new one.

Should I move my coins after restoring?

If the lost device or seed could be in someone else's hands, yes. A restore gives you access; only a move to new keys makes the lost copy worthless.

What do I need to recover a multisig wallet?

Enough keys to meet the threshold (two of three for 2-of-3) and the wallet's descriptor. With both, any multisig-capable wallet can rebuild it.
